intro:100: Surah Al-Adiyat brings together a scene full of movement and effort, and a soul held back by ingratitude and love of wealth. It then brings both before the Day when the secrets within hearts will be exposed. A person may have recited this surah since childhood while still being unsure what Arabic words such as ḍabḥ (panting), qadḥ (striking sparks), naqʿ (rising dust) and kanūd (deeply ungrateful) mean. Familiarity with its sound is not enough: we need to understand what its words convey and consider where we stand in relation to the meanings it presents.

The surah has been described as Makkan, which is the view of most commentators, and as Madinan, the view preferred by Ibn Ashur. Its short verses, swift rhythm, and general address concerning humanity and resurrection fit the Makkan view. The Madinan view draws on its portrayal of cavalry engaged in jihad and on a report about an expedition sent by the Prophet ﷺ: when news of it was delayed, according to that report, these verses revealed what its horses had done. However, the report about this occasion of revelation is weak. That story cannot therefore be asserted as the established reason for revelation, nor does understanding the surah depend on it. [Ibn Ashur, Al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr, introduction to Surah Al-Adiyat.]

Surahs reach the heart through different openings. Some invite reflection through the disconnected letters, while others enter their subject directly. Surah Muhammad, for example, opens with Allah’s words: «Those who disbelieve and prevent others from Allah’s way, He will render their deeds void» [Muhammad 47:1]. Here, the picture begins not with stationary horses whose riders are preparing to mount, but with horses already galloping. Reflecting on the surah resembles entering a walled garden: remaining outside does not reveal its fruit. Someone who enters discovers its beauty as they move among its different parts and consider how they connect.

The first five verses follow one another with the Arabic conjunction fa, and their short endings come in quick succession: ḍabḥan [ضبحا], qadḥan [قدحا], ṣubḥan [صبحا], naqʿan [نقعا] and jamʿan [جمعا]. Their sound suits the speed of the scene. We first hear the galloping, then see flashes of sparks, then the clarity of morning, and then dust obscuring part of the field. After this, the sound lengthens in la-kanūd [لكنود], la-shahīd [لشهيد] and la-shadīd [لشديد], as though the reader has entered a different reality. Finally, the forceful words describing the scattering of what lies in graves and the bringing forth of what lies in hearts awaken anyone absorbed in stillness and attachment to worldly life.

The contrast is not merely between bodily movement and stillness. The surah reveals what a blessing produces in its recipient: do they devote it to obeying their Lord, or keep it for themselves? Nor does outward activity exempt its doer from scrutiny of their intention. The passage moves from visible giving, to an inward barrier, to an accounting in which the true motive for giving or withholding cannot remain hidden.
100:1: «By the galloping, panting horses[1]» is an oath by those that run swiftly. Their quality is mentioned without explicitly naming the creatures themselves, which has given rise to different interpretations: some understood them as the camels of pilgrimage, while others understood them as horses galloping in jihad. Most commentators hold the latter view, on which this connected portrayal of panting, striking sparks and raiding is based. The plural brings to mind horses charging together, rather than a solitary animal. The honor accorded to them also relates to the riders directing them and the purpose for which they have set out.

Ḍabḥ [الضبح] is the sound of horses breathing as they gallop intensely, rather than the ordinary neighing heard in other circumstances. Ibn Abbas is reported to have described it as a sound produced when their running becomes strenuous. We hear the effect of exertion in their breathing before we can make out the details of the scene. They are not running at an easy pace; they are expending their strength. We can understand this by considering how a person’s breathing changes when running quickly compared with sitting still.

Sound has a particular effect when it precedes sight. Someone may hear movement in the darkness, become more attentive, and wait to discover where it comes from and where it is heading. This portrayal likewise begins with the sound of horses. The next verse supplies flashes of light, and then morning arrives. The whole picture is not presented at once: each part opens onto the next, making the reader feel that they are following an event rather than a static description.

One point for reflection is that the surah begins with the horses already galloping, without describing the preliminaries of mounting and preparation. This highlights responsiveness and continuing readiness, rather than every good deed requiring a fresh start after a long interruption. In the Prophet’s ﷺ description of some of the best ways of living, he mentions a man holding his horse’s reins in Allah’s cause, who «flies on its back whenever he hears the war cry or the command to face the enemy; he flies to it» [Muslim 1889]. The reins are what the rider uses to control the horse, while the cry described in the report calls for assistance. The picture is one of readiness that enables a swift response, rather than prolonged waiting that makes beginning increasingly difficult.

A person may become so accustomed to inactivity that moving from it to action becomes difficult. They may imagine that more time spent idle will prepare them, only to find that it increases their hesitation. A moving car whose direction can be changed more easily than a stationary car can be set in motion offers an illustration of the effect of sustained responsiveness. The lesson is not to deprive oneself of rest, but to avoid making inactivity a settled condition in which every act of obedience is postponed.

The oath is not by horses simply because they are horses, but by them as they gallop for this purpose. This shows that the value of a means is not determined by its outward form alone, but by what it is used for. A person may use their car, money or equipment to support the religion and serve people, or turn those same possessions into a means of boasting. The honor here lies in putting a blessing to good use, not merely owning it.

The effect of different uses becomes clearer when we consider the horses in the account of Sulayman, peace be upon him: «He then said, “I gave preference to the love of fine things over the remembrance of my Lord,” until the sun went out of sight», followed by «[He ordered], “Bring them back to me,” and he began striking [their] shanks and necks[14]» [Sad 38:32–33]. According to one interpretation of the account, the wiping mentioned means cutting the horses’ legs and necks because they had distracted him. On that reading, attachment to horses that turns someone away from remembrance differs from preparing them for obedience. This is one interpretation of the account, not a unanimously accepted explanation. The relevant point is that the significance of a blessing changes according to its connection with servitude to Allah.

The Prophet ﷺ explained this difference: «Horses are three: they are a burden for a man, a shield for another man, and a reward for a third man» [Al-Bukhari 2860; Muslim 987]. Horses that bring their owner reward are those kept ready in Allah’s cause. Good deeds are recorded for what they eat in the pasture and drink from a river, even if the owner did not intend to give them water when they passed it. Their tracks when they run also count, and the hadith even mentions their dung and urine. These details extend beyond the moment of fighting to everything involved in preparing and caring for this means.

Horses that provide a protection are kept for their owner’s needs and self-sufficiency, without neglecting Allah’s rights concerning them. Those that bring a burden of sin are kept for pride, ostentation and hostility towards Muslims. [Al-Bukhari 2371; Muslim 987.] Owning something worldly does not necessarily make it a source of harm to its owner, nor does its mere presence automatically earn reward. A person may pursue a profession such as medicine for a permissible need, combine that with an intention to benefit people, or seek to feel superior to them. These are different aims. An intention to benefit others is not just a claim contradicted by one’s actions; it is confirmed by using one’s abilities appropriately.

This opens the heart to seeking reward for the means through which it serves good, including the expenditure and care needed to maintain them. A good deed is not limited to its final form as others see it. If what horses eat and drink, and the traces of their steps, are counted, a servant should not belittle sincere efforts to prepare something beneficial. Such precise accounting does not omit what escapes people’s notice.
100:2: «striking sparks of fire [with their hooves][2]». Īrāʾ [الإيراء] means bringing fire into view, while qadḥ [القدح] means striking one thing against another so that a spark emerges. On the interpretation that the charging creatures are horses, their hooves strike stones and produce sparks as they gallop. The same usage appears in Allah’s words: «Have you thought about the fire that you kindle» [Al-Waqi‘ah 56:71]. In Arabic, qadaḥa fa-awrā means that someone struck and obtained the desired fire, while qadaḥa fa-aṣlada means that no fire came forth. The word qaddāḥah, for a lighter, comes from this usage. The wording portrays the effect of friction, not a steady fire or a lamp illuminating the entire road.

One name for these tiny sparks is nār al-ḥubāḥib. A story told to explain this expression describes an exceptionally miserly man who lit only a small fire at night so that guests would not see it. This contrasts with someone who displays their fire to guide those in need and travelers towards food. His fire thus became proverbial for weakness and concealment. [Ibn Manzur, Lisān al-ʿArab, entry ḥ-b-ḥ-b.] The purpose of this linguistic anecdote is to illustrate the smallness of the sparks and their brief appearance.

The visibility of the sparks in this portrayal suggests the darkness of night, when a small light can be discerned; morning is then explicitly mentioned in the next verse. The movement does not stop when sparks appear. The stones struck by the hooves are not the end of the road. The scene brings together inward exertion, audible in breathing, an outward obstacle of rock and darkness, and the effect of friction—yet the galloping continues through them all.

Obstacles can thus be understood as things a person may encounter on the path of obedience, rather than sufficient reason to abandon it at the first difficulty. Allah says: «Yet he did not make his way through the steep path[3]» [Al-Balad 90:11], and «Have you seen the one who turned away [from Islam]» «who gave a little, and then stopped» [An-Najm 53:33–34]. The meaning of ikdāʾ is illustrated by someone digging until they encounter a kudyah—hard ground or a rock—and then stop digging. The problem is not that the road contains difficulty, but that the very first obstacle ends all the giving that had begun.

The repeated conjunction fa in fa-l-mūriyāt [فالموريات] and what follows suits the connected actions and their rapid succession. In a life of obedience, this can be applied by moving from one good deed to another, as in Allah’s words: «They used to hasten in doing good deeds» [Al-Anbiya 21:90]. The expression fī al-khayrāt [في الخيرات], meaning within good deeds, evokes someone whose relationship with goodness is not a brief visit, but a movement among its many opportunities. They finish praying with the intention of visiting someone ill, then turn to another way of helping. Such variety helps sustain that connection, rather than allowing inactivity to swallow up the effect of every act of obedience.

The hadith states: «And a prayer followed by a prayer with no worldly talk during the gap between them will be recorded in Illiyyun» [Abu Dawud 558; hasan]. This glad tiding must not be separated from its condition that there be no idle talk between the prayers. The point is a continuing connection with Allah, not merely a succession of outward acts. Allah’s words convey a related meaning: «So whenever you are free[5], strive in worship» [Ash-Sharh 94:7]. Finishing something should not bring every aspiration to an end, but offer an opportunity to move on to work pleasing to Allah.
100:3: «launching raids at dawn[3]» reveals the destination of the horses whose breathing we have heard and whose hooves we have seen strike sparks: carrying their riders, they raid the enemy in the morning. Connecting this scene to what precedes it suggests a journey through the night that reaches its destination at dawn. Neither the darkness of the road nor the length of the journey has ended the mission. The conjunction fa links arrival with action, rather than making arrival an occasion for a break that defeats the purpose.

Anas reported that the Prophet ﷺ would raid after dawn and listen for the call to prayer. If he heard it, he refrained; otherwise, he attacked. [Muslim 382.] On the day of Khaybar, he said: «when we approach a nation (i.e. enemy to fight) then miserable is the morning of the warned ones» [Al-Bukhari 2991]. The Qur’an states: «When it[45] descends on their courtyard, how terrible will be the morning of those who were warned» [As-Saffat 37:177]. These references clarify the connection between morning and the raid in this scene. They retain the picture within its context, rather than turning the mention of time into a meaning detached from the action.

The lesson is not to glorify exhaustion for its own sake, but to avoid making every experience of fatigue an excuse to neglect the purpose for which one began. Rest that helps a person fulfill their work differs from postponement repeated whenever the point of responsibility draws near. This reflection moves the soul from waiting for ideal circumstances to doing what it can, without treating the difficulty of the road as an unexpected discovery that overturns its resolve.

The portrayal of horses advancing towards the enemy connects with the subject known in Islamic jurisprudence as jihād al-ṭalab, as distinct from reducing warfare solely to waiting for an enemy to attack. Here, the scene depicts setting out and raiding in Allah’s cause against those who obstruct His path. A general lesson about acting and giving is then drawn from it, without erasing its original setting by treating the entire picture as metaphorical. This passage is not a detailed account of the rulings and conditions governing that subject.
100:4: «stirring up thereby clouds of dust»: the horses stir up dust; naqʿ [النقع] means rising dust. To stir something up is to move it after it has been still, so the dust itself bears witness to the force of the galloping and advance. There are two interpretations of the pronoun in bihi [به]. It may refer to the place of the raid, meaning that they stirred up dust there, or to the galloping, meaning that they raised it through their running. In the first reading, the preposition relates to place; in the second, to cause. Both preserve the picture of movement that has reached the ground of confrontation.

After morning has brought light, part of the scene becomes obscured again, this time by dust rather than the darkness of night. The meaning of the dust extends beyond the beauty of a picture observed from afar: it is the effect of effort experienced by those within the event. The horses do not arrive and remain motionless at its edge. There is charging and withdrawing, and dust rises. Someone who wants to work without any effect on their comfort or appearance has imposed conditions on the path of giving unlike those portrayed here.

In contrast, Surah At-Tawbah presents the conditions demanded by those reluctant to act: «If it had been an easy win within reach and a short journey, those [hypocrites] would have followed you, but the distance seemed too far for them» [At-Tawbah 9:42], and their words: «Do not march forth in this heat[67]» [At-Tawbah 9:81]. They want an immediate benefit, a short and easy journey, and weather that brings no hardship. The same attitude may recur in someone who professes readiness to serve the religion on condition that they suffer not the slightest harm. The problem is not an inability to do anything at all, but making one’s response conditional on guaranteed comfort and gain together.

This is why feet becoming dusty has significance in the Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Anyone whose feet get covered with dust in the cause of Allah will not be touched by the Fire» [Al-Bukhari 2811]. What people may regard as a change in appearance can be, before Allah, the trace of sincere effort. The purpose is not to seek dust itself, but to avoid rejecting obedience because it will leave some mark on the body or clothing. What matters is that it be in Allah’s cause, not merely becoming dirty.

In the account of the boy and the monk, when the monk recognized what the boy had attained, he told him: «You will be put to trial» [Muslim 3005]. His teaching did not promise a path free from trials; it prepared the boy to understand them. The Prophet ﷺ also said: «The Paradise is surrounded by hardships and the Hell-Fire is surrounded by temptations» [Muslim 2822]. Knowing that the path may involve hardship helps one endure it. Someone who has imagined a promise that nothing will obstruct them may stop at the first obstacle. If a journey involves no effort whatsoever, that may invite an examination of what its traveler is actually giving, rather than treating mere comfort as proof of perfect progress.
100:5: «plunging thereby into the midst of the enemy[4]»: the horses and their riders reach the middle of the enemy’s gathered force rather than stopping at its edge. The succession of actions ends at the furthest point in the picture: audible galloping, visible sparks, a morning raid, dust, and finally entry into the midst of the gathering. This is not abundant movement without direction, but sustained movement reaching the point of confrontation intended by the riders.

This contrasts with the picture of someone who worships Allah on an edge. Allah says: «There are some people who worship Allah on the edge [of faith][6]: if something good comes to them, they are content; but if they are afflicted with a trial, they turn back[7]» [Al-Hajj 22:11]. One illustration is a person who remains at the edge of the army: if spoils appear, they join in; if hardship appears, they retreat. Such a person reserves an escape route whenever the path conflicts with their desires. Someone whose certainty in Allah’s promise is firmly established does not make immediate gain the sole reason for remaining, keeping in mind Allah’s words: «Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth, and in return they will have Paradise[82]» [At-Tawbah 9:111].

The word jamʿan [جمعا] evokes a confrontation not with scattered individuals, but with a force gathered and ready to meet them. The Qur’an states: «Soon their united front will be defeated, and they will flee[16]» [Al-Qamar 54:45]. This reminds us that the enemy’s gathering does not place it beyond Allah’s power. It does not identify the battle portrayed in Surah Al-Adiyat; it simply shows that the word for a gathered force conveys something different from encountering a few individuals.

The description of the battle then stops without stating its outcome: was it followed by victory, death or captivity? This ending is not mentioned, just as the preliminaries of mounting were omitted at the surah’s beginning. One point for reflection is that the focus here lies in genuine giving and faithfulness, rather than making an action’s value depend on an immediate worldly result. Allah says: «for whoever fights in the way of Allah, whether he is killed or attains victory, We will give him a great reward» [An-Nisa 4:74]. Being killed is mentioned before prevailing, while the promise of reward remains connected in both cases to fighting in Allah’s cause.

This changes the question a person asks about their work. Instead of stopping at ‘When will I see results?’, they ask whether they have given what was required of them and faithfully followed the path to its intended point. A person may not live to see the full outcome they hope for; that alone does not show that their effort was wasted. Sincerity remains a necessary condition. The surah’s conclusion returns to what lies within hearts, so outward boldness alone does not provide a final endorsement of its possessor.
100:6: The statement affirmed by the oath comes after the flowing scene: «indeed, man is very ungrateful to his Lord[5]». The Arabic particles inna and la emphasize the judgment, while the lengthening verse ending marks a transition from swift giving to a settled condition of ingratitude. Some understood ‘the human being’ here as the disbeliever or the wicked person; others understood it as a description of what tends to dominate the human soul when it does not struggle against its faults and purify itself. We should not begin by reading the verse as something that cannot concern us, but examine our own gratitude for what we have received.

Kanūd [الكنود] means deeply ungrateful and denying blessings. One aspect of its meaning is receiving blessings without producing the fruit of gratitude. This is illustrated by land described as kanūd: it is watered but grows nothing, unlike responsive land that yields abundant fruit when watered. The contrast does not concern the presence of a blessing alone. Both people may have received gifts, but one puts what they have to use, while the other keeps it for themselves. They may possess time, strength and equipment, yet devote none of them to something beneficial.

Kanūd has also been explained as someone who counts misfortunes and forgets blessings. They keep an exact account of what they have missed while overlooking the gifts amid which they live, so that abundance turns into a constant sense of lack. The point is not to deny the pain they experience, but to expose an imbalance in perspective: the misfortune is kept in memory, the blessing erased from it, and the resulting heart fails to see what calls for gratitude.

A report describing the kanūd speaks of someone who eats alone, withholds assistance and beats his slave. [At-Tabarani, Al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr 7984; weak as a report attributed to the Prophet ﷺ.] Rafd [الرفد] means a gift or assistance. The picture combines keeping food to oneself, withholding benefit and mistreating someone weaker.

The phrase li-rabbihi [لربه], towards his Lord, makes this ingratitude still more grievous. The person denies the right of the One who has nurtured them through blessings, not someone who has never treated them generously. They may be kind to a friend or spend freely on their own interests, but respond to obedience to Allah with reluctance and withholding. The possessive pronoun brings the matter close: it is their own Lord who has favored them personally. These are not distant blessings unrelated to them. How, then, can a blessing become a means of enjoyment alone, while its Giver’s right is forgotten?

A person may be highly intelligent and energetic in worldly affairs, asking, learning and researching until they attain their aim, then excuse themselves in religion by saying that they do not know where to begin or from whom to learn. The claim of inability is not equivalent in the two cases: they have demonstrated an ability to ask questions and take practical steps in the first, but neglected both in the second. One form of self-examination is to consider the blessings of speech, intellect, wealth and equipment. Has the tongue become capable of every conversation except explaining what is good, and the mind attentive to every interest except understanding what pleases Allah? This takes gratitude from a general expression to actually using what Allah has bestowed.
100:7: There are two interpretations of the pronoun in «and he himself is a witness to that[6]»: the human being bears witness to their own ingratitude, the more prominent reading in this explanation; or Allah is witness to it. The first highlights a person’s knowledge of their own actions, while the second highlights that they cannot hide from their Lord. In either case, manufactured excuses cannot serve as a covering that erases the reality of ingratitude.

A person’s testimony against themselves includes what they know of their condition in this world and what will testify against them on the Day of Resurrection. They may privately know that they could have given but did not, or recognized a blessing without showing gratitude, then try to evade this acknowledgment. On the Day of Accounting, they may appeal to ignorance or inability, only for their own limbs to testify against them. The hypocrites’ reported excuse, «If we had known there was fighting, we would have certainly followed you» [Al Imran 3:167], illustrates words intended to justify staying behind. Merely saying them is of no use when they contradict what the speaker knows about themselves.

Self-examination may begin as a reproach within the heart. If a person resents it, they may occupy themselves so that they no longer hear it. In a hadith, the caller who warns against violating Allah’s limits is described as «Allah's admonishment in the heart of every Muslim» [Ahmad 17634]. The problem may not be that the admonition has failed to reach someone, but that they do not want it to retain a voice. Faith in the Hereafter strengthens this willingness to reconsider oneself, rather than prompting a person to silence everything that reminds them of their responsibility.

Resurrection and the self-reproaching soul are mentioned together in Allah’s words: «I swear by the Day of Resurrection» «and I swear by the self-reproaching soul[1]» [Al-Qiyamah 75:1–2], followed by «But man desires to persist in sin[2]» [Al-Qiyamah 75:5]. One lesson is that someone who wants unrestricted license to sin resents what reproaches them, even if that reproach comes from within. Keeping the accounting in mind, however, leaves the heart willing to question its choices. The relief someone feels after silencing their own reproach is therefore no proof that their action was innocent.

Another aspect of this testimony is that people recognize shortcomings when they look at others. An authentic statement from Abu Hurayrah describes someone who notices a speck in his brother’s eye but forgets the large piece of wood, or trunk, in his own. [Al-Bukhari, Al-Adab al-Mufrad 592; authentic as a statement of the Companion, not a Prophetic saying.] A qadhāh [القذاة] is a small object that falls into the eye, while a jidhʿ [الجذع] is a large piece of wood. The example depicts close attention to another person’s fault alongside blindness to a greater fault in oneself. A person knows that someone else has failed to fulfill a right or give what they could, yet gathers excuses when the question reaches them. This ability to criticize reveals that they know the standard they try to suspend when judging themselves.
100:8: «and he is truly extreme in his love of wealth» exposes a barrier behind ingratitude: love of wealth that has become so powerful that it governs a person’s choices. Khayr [الخير] here means wealth, as in the words concerning a bequest, «if he leaves behind any wealth» [Al-Baqarah 2:180], which some understood there as abundant wealth. The meaning is not that everything a person calls good prevents obedience, nor that owning wealth is itself blameworthy. The subject is an attachment that directs all blessings towards self-interest and withholds them from fulfilling Allah’s rights.

There are several closely related interpretations of la-shadīd [لشديد]: intense love of wealth, miserliness caused by that love, or great strength and eagerness when pursuing worldly matters. A linguistic illustration is that the Arabic pattern faʿīl can carry a passive meaning, as jarīḥ [جريح] means wounded, majrūḥ [مجروح], and rajīm [رجيم] means pelted, marjūm [مرجوم]. The shadīd can thus be pictured as someone bound tightly by wealth and encircled by its restraints. Another explanation is that he ties up and closes the containers holding his wealth, refusing to open them for giving. These readings show how love becomes withholding, rather than remaining a mere inward feeling.

The hadith gives this condition a concrete image by comparing the miser and the giver to two men wearing iron coats. The giver’s coat expands, whereas whenever the miser wishes to spend, each ring clings to its place: «he tries to expand it, but it does not expand» [Al-Bukhari 1443]. The barrier is like a tight garment restraining its wearer, even though the money is already in his hand. Allah’s words offer a related picture: «who amasses wealth and counts it over and again[1]» [Al-Humazah 104:2]. The person becomes absorbed in collecting, counting and shutting things away, instead of making the blessing a means of benefiting someone beyond themselves.

Here the difference between outward obstacles and an inward barrier becomes clear. The horses encountered rocks, darkness and fatigue, yet continued, whereas a person may remain seated amid abundant means because their soul refuses to give. A concise way to describe this barrier is miserliness with oneself and one’s pleasures: withholding oneself and one’s effort, or the comfort and enjoyment one has become accustomed to. Not every obstacle outside the soul is imaginary. Nevertheless, overcoming the inward barrier may open doors that a person had thought closed.

It is therefore striking how many burdens upon the soul the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge from: «O Allah! I seek refuge with You from worry and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from being heavily in debt and from being overpowered by (other) men» [Al-Bukhari 6369]. This supplication gathers worry, grief, inability, laziness, cowardice and miserliness, followed by the weight of debt and being overpowered by people. Seeking help concerns not only surrounding circumstances, but also what may bind the heart before its possessor even begins to act.

This meaning extends from the individual to the community. Before the account of Talut and Jalut in Surah Al-Baqarah comes the scene of «those who left their homes, while they were in thousands for fear of death» [Al-Baqarah 2:243], followed by encouragement to lend a goodly loan and Allah’s words: «It is Allah Who withholds and gives in abundance» [Al-Baqarah 2:245]. Numbers alone do not remove fear. In nurturing the heart, two foundations are recalled: life and death are in Allah’s hands, and so are the expansion and restriction of provision. These address fear for one’s life and fear for one’s wealth before confronting a demanding responsibility.

Then come the words of the leaders of the Children of Israel to a prophet of theirs: «Appoint for us a king so that we fight in the way of Allah» [Al-Baqarah 2:246]. One way to reflect on this sequence is to contrast a people who set out fleeing death with a people asking for someone to unite them in fulfilling their duty. Change begins with the direction that becomes settled in people’s souls. A tyrant may exploit people’s fear for their lives and possessions to preserve his rule, with part of his intimidating power residing within their hearts. Reform therefore cannot be separated from addressing that fear. Abundant numbers and resources are insufficient when people have inwardly surrendered.

In the hadith about nations gathering against Muslims, the Prophet ﷺ explained that the cause is not necessarily their small number. They may be numerous yet afflicted by wahn, which he explained as love of worldly life and hatred of death. [Abu Dawud 4297; authentic.] The diagnosis moves beyond counting what people possess to examining what possesses their hearts. Strength may appear plentiful outwardly, then be disabled by fear that places every immediate interest ahead of the duty it should serve.

A familiar picture of this heaviness is someone wishing to rise for night prayer or Fajr, only to be held back by the warmth of the bed and laziness, as though restraints stood between them and getting up. Alongside this, we may recall the Qur’anic description: «what is the matter with you that when you are asked to march forth in the cause of Allah, you cling heavily to the earth[37]» [At-Tawbah 9:38]. The weight of attachment pulls a person towards what they have become accustomed to. The comparison concerns reluctance and heaviness, not an assertion that every kind of religious responsibility is identical.

The hadith describes Satan tying three knots at the back of a sleeping person’s head. When the person wakes and remembers Allah, one knot comes undone; when they perform ablution, another comes undone; and when they pray, another comes undone, so that they enter the morning energetic and in good spirits. [Al-Bukhari 1142.] Breaking the first barrier is therefore not the end of the path. A person may get up, remember Allah or perform ablution, then return to bed claiming there is still time, and lose what they had begun. This picture restores the importance of connecting one action to the next: completing what removes the restraints, rather than abandoning the work after an initial response.

The Prophet ﷺ brought two contrasting pictures together in one hadith: «Wretched is the slave of the dinar! Wretched is the slave of the dirham! Wretched is the slave of Khamīsah (a kind of fine garments)!» He described this person as follows: «If given, he is pleased, but if not, he is displeased». On the other side, he said: «Tūba (a tree in Paradise) is for a slave who holds the reins of his horse to strive in Allah's cause, with his hair unkempt and feet covered with dust» [Al-Bukhari 2887]. A khamīṣah is a garment, so the problem is not confined to coins. Clothing, possessions or appearance may also enslave a person. Satisfaction when given something and anger when it is withheld reveal the direction around which the heart has come to revolve.

The first person is also described with the words: «May he be wretched and may he relapse, and if he is pierced with a thorn, may he not find anyone to take it out for him» [Al-Bukhari 2887]. This means that if a thorn pierces him, may it not be removed. It is a supplication against him, and brings to mind someone whose smallest obstacle turns them away from everything they intended. In contrast, the other person does not make disheveled hair and dusty feet the end of their work. Preserving appearance and comfort no longer solely governs their response. The contrast is between a man restrained by his possessions and another whom the traces of giving do not prevent from remaining faithful.

The hadith continues its description of the second person: «if he is appointed as a guard, he accepts his post with satisfaction»; and, concerning the other assignment, «if he is appointed in the rearward, he accepts his post with satisfaction», and then «if he asks for permission, he is not permitted, and if he intercedes, his intercession is not accepted» [Al-Bukhari 2887]. The sāqah is the rear of the army. He diligently performs the task assigned to him, instead of working in one place while his heart longs for a more conspicuous position. He may lack the standing that opens doors or secures acceptance of an intercession among people, yet being unknown to them does not prevent sincerity in his work.

Love of worldly life may grow within the soul little by little, like a spreading illness that takes over different parts of it, until the person considers everything solely in terms of their own gain and comfort. The effect of one’s environment can be illustrated by a setting in which a particular blight thrives. Constant preoccupation with worldly life, without self-examination or stepping out to give, prepares the soul for traits it did not initially intend to acquire. The comparison illustrates the effect of immersion and repetition, rather than merely condemning the permissible needs of life.

Warning against even the intention of jihad dying away, the Prophet ﷺ taught that someone who dies without having fought and without having contemplated fighting dies with a branch of hypocrisy. [Muslim 1910; meaning conveyed indirectly.] The hadith combines not taking part in an expedition with not contemplating it. The point is the danger of inward surrender that leaves neither readiness nor desire to fulfill what is right. Its wording does not pass judgment on everyone from whom a particular outward action has not been seen; it warns against the specific condition it describes.

The freedom intended here is for the soul to become free of whatever prevents servitude to Allah. The words of Imran’s wife offer an illustration: «My Lord, I dedicate to You what is in my womb[15]» [Al Imran 3:35]. One lesson drawn from muḥarraran [محررا] is to free one’s direction towards Allah from competing restraints. A person may think they have escaped responsibility, only to become enslaved to their own desires or what they expect from others. The more truthful their servitude to Allah, the less power wealth, habit and status have over their choices. They own things and benefit from them, without allowing those things to own their decisions.
100:9: «Does he not know that when the contents of graves will be overturned» takes the person from constant preoccupation with what they collect and preserve to the fate that none of their accumulated possessions can avert. Someone who begrudged every effort that might cost them life’s comforts will become a body in a grave, then be brought out for accounting. Baʿtharah [البعثرة] evokes disturbing and bringing out what had been settled. Neither the stillness the person was accustomed to nor the place where their body was hidden can shield them from resurrection.

The wording is mā fī al-qubūr [ما في القبور], ‘what is in the graves’, rather than man fī al-qubūr, ‘who is in the graves’. One explanation relates this to the condition of bodies after death, when they are no longer in the state of living, reasoning people. Reflection brings out the collapse of appearances and titles through which a person once magnified themselves. The life whose possessions they thought it their ultimate purpose to preserve ends in this narrow enclosure, then in a scattering they cannot prevent. Wealth cannot interrupt the road between a person and their grave, however expansive it makes their worldly life.

In the order of the mushaf, Al-Adiyat stands between Az-Zalzalah and Al-Qari‘ah. One way to consider this proximity is that deeply rooted love of wealth needs something that shakes the standards of heedlessness and strikes the heart with the scene of the Hereafter. Az-Zalzalah closes with seeing an atom’s weight of good and evil. [Az-Zalzalah 99:7–8.] Keeping this accounting in mind changes how a person evaluates what they give. A similar reflection arises from Al-Asr standing between At-Takathur and Al-Humazah: preoccupation with competing for more, and preoccupation with finding fault and mocking others, with the judgment of loss between them. These are reflective connections that help us receive the surahs together, not a restriction of their purposes to a single interpretation.
100:10: The unveiling does not end when bodies emerge: «and the secrets of the hearts will be brought to light[7]». Taḥṣīl [التحصيل] can be illustrated by extracting grain from its husk through a process that reveals what was inside. Likewise, concealed intentions and motives are brought out from the heart. What appeared mixed or indistinguishable to people—sincerity and ostentation, seeking truth or seeking praise—will no longer remain hidden behind an action’s outward form. What lies in graves is scattered, what lies in hearts is brought forth, and the accounting encompasses the human being outwardly and inwardly.

The warning therefore addresses the active person too, not only the ungrateful one. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about a man who fights out of bravery, another who fights out of partisan zeal, and another who fights to be seen: which of them is fighting in Allah’s cause? He replied: «Whoever fights so that the word of Allah be supreme is indeed in the cause of Allah» [Muslim 1904]. Sharing the outward form of fighting does not make their purposes equal, and courage alone is insufficient evidence of sincerity. When reading the scene of Al-Adiyat, a person should not stop at ‘Did I act?’ but also ask, ‘For what purpose did I act?’

The hadith about the first people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection describes a man who fought to be called brave, a man who acquired knowledge and recited the Qur’an to be called a scholar and reciter, and a man who spent to be called generous. Each had his actual intention exposed, and the outward form of the deed he claimed to have done for Allah did not benefit him. [Muslim 1905.] Scrutiny of intention is thus not confined to wealth or fighting: it includes learning, teaching, recitation and spending. The purpose is for the obedient person to return to truthfulness with Allah, rather than being satisfied with people’s praise for what they have seen.
100:11: «Indeed, their Lord is All-Aware of them on that Day[8]» closes the surah with Allah’s encompassing knowledge of His servants’ true condition. The knowledge described here highlights hidden matters and motives, not merely an action’s visible form. He knows what prompted each person to move and what prompted them to stop, which blessings they were grateful for and which they denied. Recompense on that Day is based on this knowledge of what they previously did, not on what they managed to reveal to or conceal from people.

No speck of dust that touched the foot of someone striving in His cause escapes Him, nor any blessing whose benefit the ungrateful person withheld, nor any intention hidden behind an action praised by others. In this connection, the Sunnah describes the merit of the changed smell of a fasting person’s breath, caused by fasting: «the smell of the mouth of the fasting person is more pleasant in the sight of Allah than the smell of musk» [Al-Bukhari 1894]. The measure is not whether people find an effect pleasant, but the reality of the deed before Allah. Sincere effort is not lost because nobody saw it, and abundant movement cannot deceive the One who knows the secrets within hearts.

It is reported that when Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was told of some of those killed whose names were unknown, he replied that Allah nevertheless knew them. [Ibn Abi Shaybah, Al-Muṣannaf, chapter ‘Sending An-Nu‘man ibn Muqarrin to Nahawand’, no. 34365 in the Dar Ar-Rushd edition.] This report illustrates the reassurance of someone who works without their standing being known among people. The knowledge whose benefit is hoped for on the Day of Accounting is not the fame of a name, but the Lord’s knowledge of its possessor’s true condition.
